summary: For ages 8-9, reasoning turns outward: children stop merely explaining their own method and begin critiquing someone else's, and they chain multiple facts into a single argument ('since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48'). Two moves define this level — building a multi-step because/therefore argument, and diagnosing WHY a peer's method fails (which step broke, not just that the answer differs). Arguments still lean on concrete referents (fraction bars, place-value equipment) but now require a because/therefore link between steps. Best taught through structured talk — analysing a deliberately flawed worked example, agreeing whether an argument 'makes sense', and asking 'which STEP is wrong and why?' rather than 'is the answer right?'
misconceptions: 'It's wrong because the answer's different from mine' — judges a peer's argument by answer-agreement rather than by finding the flawed step
Checking one example and treating the rule as proved for all cases
Restating the method louder instead of giving a reason why it works
Believing a longer fraction/denominator names a bigger piece (1/5 > 1/3)

activities.title: Convince-me dialogue: catch the broken step
steps: Listen to or read a plausible-but-wrong worked chain, e.g. a partner says: 'I did 71 minus 46. I couldn't do 1 take 6, so I did 6 take 1, that's 5, then 7 take 4 is 3, so 35.'
Point to the EXACT line where the thinking first goes wrong (the digit-flip), rather than re-solving and comparing totals.
Say WHY that line breaks, grounded in place value: 'you can't flip the digits; the 1 is really part of 71, so you exchange a ten to make 11, and 11 take 6 is 5.'
When challenged with 'how do you know?' or 'why does exchanging fix it?', keep going until the objection becomes a because-chain.
Then construct a correct chain aloud for 71 − 46, starting from what 71 really is (giving 25).
activities.insight: Critiquing someone else's error forces your own reasoning to become explicit: a vague 'that's not right' can be turned, under questioning, into a because-chain you did not know you had.

activities.title: Build-an-argument workspace: chain the facts, mark the flaw
steps: Assemble fact tiles ('6×10=60', '6×2=12') into a because/therefore sequence and write the linking reason, e.g. 'since 6×10=60 and 6×2=12, then 6×8=60−12=48.'
In a separate flawed worked example (a column subtraction with a mis-recorded exchange), tap or mark the single broken step and write or pick why it fails.
Check your own chain reads as 'since… and… therefore…', not just a list of true facts side by side.
activities.insight: A string of true facts only becomes an argument when because/therefore links them; locating 'which step, and why' is a concrete, repeatable move.

activities.title: Fraction-bar size argument: 1/3 > 1/5
steps: Using fraction bars or an area model showing the same whole split into 3 and into 5, state and justify which piece is bigger.
Build the chain: 'more equal parts means smaller pieces, so fifths are smaller than thirds, therefore 1/3 > 1/5.'
When a classmate claims '1/5 is bigger because 5 is bigger than 3', find and explain the flaw using the shared bar both of you can point at.
activities.insight: Splitting the same whole into MORE equal parts makes each part SMALLER, so a unit fraction with the larger denominator is the smaller number — and a representation both parties can point at keeps a critique about the reasoning, not the person.

activities.title: When is a check really a proof? Convince a doubter
steps: Given a general claim and a single example that fits it, decide whether checking that one example proves the claim for all cases.
Explain why one confirming example is not a proof, and what would be needed to be convinced for every case.
Evaluate a weak check such as: 'A classmate says 71 − 46 = 35 is fine because 35 + 46 is close to 71. Is that a good way to check? What does it actually tell you?'
activities.insight: Evidence that falls short of a complete argument — a single confirming example, or an approximate 'close to' check — does not establish or verify a claim; distinguishing 'it works here / it's roughly right' from 'it must always work / it is exactly right' is a key step toward justification.

activities.title: Compare-and-annotate launch: sound vs flawed argument
steps: Study a side-by-side pair of worked arguments for the same problem — one sound, one with a hidden error.
Tap each step to reveal the reason it does or does not follow, then say in your own words which argument holds and where the other breaks.
Use this only as a springboard: afterwards, construct your OWN correct chain or critique a fresh flawed example aloud.
activities.insight: Seeing a correct and a flawed argument side by side can seed critique and vocabulary for 'why a step follows', but reading annotations is only a starting point for producing your own argument.

checkQuestion: Here is how a classmate worked out 71 − 46. They wrote: '1 take away 6 — I can't, so I'll do 6 take away 1, that's 5. Then 7 take away 4 is 3. So the answer is 35.' Is their thinking okay? Talk me through what they did, step by step, and tell me where — if anywhere — it goes wrong and why.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child locating the specific faulty STEP (flipping 1−6 into 6−1 instead of exchanging a ten) AND giving a reason grounded in place value (the 1 is part of 71, so you take a ten to make 11, then 11−6=5), rather than just announcing that 35 is the wrong answer.
